concept.name: Maker fee
concept.definition: The charge (or, on maker-taker venues, typically a rebate) applied to an execution that adds liquidity - i.e., a resting order that is traded against. In classic U.S. equity maker-taker pricing the 'maker' is paid a rebate rather than charged; on taker-maker venues and most crypto exchanges the maker pays a (usually smaller) fee.
concept.intuition: The maker posts and waits; the venue prices that patience differently from aggression - sometimes rewarding it, sometimes charging less for it.
concept.mechanics: Exchanges publish per-share/per-contract schedules distinguishing adding from removing liquidity; e.g., Nasdaq pays tiered per-share rebates for displayed liquidity added (around $0.0018-$0.00305 depending on volume tier) while charging for removal. Whether an execution is maker or taker is determined by which side rested in the book first.
concept.failure_modes: Maker economics distort order placement: traders post sub-optimally priced orders to harvest rebates, and queue formaker status can mean missed fills that cost more than the rebate earned. Fee tiers also make marginal costs volume-dependent and opaque to end clients.
concept.misconceptions: 'Maker fee' on U.S. equity exchanges is usually negative - a rebate - while on crypto venues makers genuinely pay a fee; the same word covers both signs. Being a maker is about resting first, not about using a limit order (a marketable limit order is a taker).
concept.example: Your resting limit sell is hit by an incoming market order; as the liquidity adder you receive Nasdaq's $0.0020-per-share add rebate instead of paying the $0.0030 removal fee.
